strings.title: Make the Next Ten
strings.label: Day 1
strings.strategy: Add up to the next ten first, then add what is left.
strings.keywords: next ten, friendly number, break apart, jump
strings.connection: First string of the week. Sets up the open number line and the idea that 10 ones make a ten.
watchFor: Counting on by ones (28, 29, 30, 31...): accept it, then ask "Is there a jump that gets you to a ten?"
Breaking the number the wrong way (28 + 5 as 28 + 3 + 2 = 33, but stopping at 31): ask "How much of the 5 have you used?"
Not knowing the partners of 10: keep a quick reference (8 and 2, 7 and 3...) and celebrate students who use them.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did the first problems help with the later ones?" Land: get to the next ten, then add the rest.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "Hold on to this."
Look for: "8 and 2 make a ten." Ask: "How does 8 + 2 help?" Model: numberline 28 +2

responses.say: 8 and 2 make a ten, so 20 and 10 is 30.
responses.tip: Click +2 and type “8 + 2 makes a ten”

problems.notes: Look for: 28 + 2 = 30, then 3 more. Ask: "Where did the 5 go?" Word choice: "I broke 5 into 2 and 3." Model: numberline 28 +2 +3

responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: where did the 5 go?
Then ask: is there a jump that gets you to a ten?
Used only part of the 5. Ask: how much of the 5 have you used?

problems.notes: Look for: 48 + 2 = 50, then 4 more. Ask: "How did you know to use 2?" Model: numberline 48 +2 +4

responses.say: I did 48 + 6 like the last one: to the next ten first.

responses.tip: Ask: how many tens are in 14?

problems.notes: Look for: 67 + 3 = 70, then 5 more. Ask: "What is the next ten after 67?" Model: numberline 67 +3 +5

responses.tip: A Day 4 strategy. Accept it and name it.

problems.notes: Look for: 67 + 3 = 70, then 15 more; or 67 + 10 + 8. Ask: "Can the last problem help?" Model: numberline 67 +3 +15

responses.say: 67 + 3 = 70, and I still had 15 left, so 85.

problems.notes: Look for: the same moves as 67 + 8. Ask: "Predict before I show it. What changed?" Model: numberline 167 +3 +5

responses.say: Same as 67 + 8, just in the hundreds: 175.
responses.tip: Ask: what changed? what stayed the same?

strings.title: Split by Place Value
strings.label: Day 2
strings.strategy: Add tens with tens and ones with ones, then put them together. When the ones make more than 10, that makes another ten.
strings.keywords: tens, ones, hundreds, place value, partial sums, make a new ten
strings.connection: Day 1 made a ten on the number line. Today the ones combine into a new ten when we add by place value.
watchFor: Saying "3 + 4" for 30 + 40: ask "Is it 3 + 4 or 30 + 40? How do you know?" and write the real values.
Writing 713 for 70 + 13: ask "How many tens are in 13? Where do they go?"
Forgetting the ones: ask "Did you add every part?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "What happened when the ones added up to more than 10?" Land: 10 ones make a new ten, and it joins the other tens.

problems.notes: Look for: 3 tens + 4 tens = 7 tens. Ask: "How many tens?"

responses.tip: Ask: 3 what? 4 what? Why the zero?

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact, or 6 + 4 + 3. Ask: "How many tens and ones is 13?"
Look for: 70 + 13 = 83. Ask: "How did the last two problems help?" Word choice: "13 ones is 1 ten and 3 ones." Model: text 36 + 47 = 30 + 40 + 6 + 7 ; = 70 + 13 ; = 83

responses.tip: The target strategy

responses.say: I said it like the last two problems.

responses.tip: Ask: how many tens are in 13? Where do they go?

problems.notes: Look for: 70 + 14. Ask: "Where does the extra ten come from?" Model: text 28 + 56 = 20 + 50 + 8 + 6 ; = 70 + 14 ; = 84

responses.tip: Day 1's strategy. Ask: which was easier?
Ask: where does the extra ten from 14 go?

problems.notes: Look for: 70 + 13, or 45 + 30 + 8 on the number line. Ask: "Did anyone do it another way?" Model: numberline 45 +30 +8
Look for: 100 + 50 + 12. Ask: "What happens to the hundreds?" Model: text 125 + 37 = 100 + 20 + 30 + 5 + 7 ; = 100 + 50 + 12 ; = 162
Look for: 400 + 70 + 13. Ask: "Which part makes a new ten?" Model: text 356 + 127 = 300 + 100 + 50 + 20 + 6 + 7 ; = 400 + 70 + 13 ; = 483

responses.say: I did ones first: 13, then 70, then 400.

responses.tip: Ask: which part makes a new ten?

strings.title: Over the Hundred
strings.label: Day 3
strings.strategy: Get to the next hundred (or ten), then add what is left. Tens can regroup into a new hundred, just like ones regroup into a ten.
strings.keywords: next hundred, friendly number, regroup, 10 tens
strings.connection: Day 1 got to the next ten. Today we get to the next hundred.
watchFor: Writing 1003 for 95 + 8: ask "Is it more or less than 200? Where is it on the line?"
Losing track of the hundreds (186 + 25 = 111): ask "About how big should the answer be?"
Breaking the number awkwardly: accept it, then ask "Which jump would get you to a hundred?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How is getting to the next hundred like getting to the next ten?" Land: 10 tens make a hundred, just like 10 ones make a ten.

problems.notes: Look for: 9 tens + 1 ten = 10 tens. Ask: "How many tens make 100?"
Look for: 95 + 5 = 100, then 3 more. Ask: "Where did you stop?" Model: numberline 95 +5 +3
Look for: the same as 95 + 8, plus 100. Ask: "What is the same? What changed?" Model: numberline 195 +5 +3
Look for: 186 + 14 = 200, then 11 more; or 186 + 20 + 5. Ask: "How did you know to use 14?" Model: numberline 186 +14 +11
Look for: 275 + 25 = 300, then 5 more. Ask: "How many tens did it take to cross 300?" Model: numberline 275 +25 +5
Look for: 275 + 25 = 300, then 13 more. Ask: "Can the last problem help?" Model: numberline 275 +25 +13
Look for: 368 + 32 = 400, then 13; or 368 + 40 + 5. Ask: "Which stops did you choose, and why?" Model: numberline 368 +32 +13

strings.title: Add a Friendly Number, Then Take Back
strings.label: Day 4
strings.strategy: When a number is close to a friendly number (a ten or a hundred), add the friendly number, then take back the extra.
strings.keywords: friendly number, close to, too much, take back
strings.connection: Days 1–3 added up to a friendly number. Today we jump past it and come back.
watchFor: Forgetting to take back (46 + 9 = 56): ask "Is 46 + 9 more or less than 46 + 10?"
Going the wrong way (46 + 9 = 57): ask the same question and show both on the line.
Taking back the wrong amount (135 + 98 = 232): ask "How far is 98 from 100?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "When is this a good strategy?" Land: when one number is close to a ten or a hundred.

problems.notes: Look for: one jump of 10. Ask: "Where did you start and land?" Model: numberline 46 +10
Look for: 46 + 10, then back 1. Ask: "Can 46 + 10 help?" Word choice: "too much by 1, take it back." Model: numberline 46 +10 -1
Look for: 46 + 20, back 1. Ask: "What is the same about 46 + 9 and 46 + 19?" Model: numberline 46 +20 -1
Look for: 46 + 30, back 1. Ask: "Predict how someone will do it." Model: numberline 46 +30 -1
Look for: 135 + 100, back 1. Ask: "Why 100?" Model: numberline 135 +100 -1
Look for: 135 + 100, back 2. Ask: "What changed from the last one?" Model: numberline 135 +100 -2
Look for: 247 + 200, back 2; or 245 + 200 (give and take). Ask: "Which friendly number did you use?" Model: numberline 247 +200 -2

strings.title: Where Does the New Ten Go?
strings.label: Day 5
strings.strategy: Connect mental strategies to the standard algorithm: the carried 1 is a new ten (or hundred) made from 10 ones (or 10 tens).
strings.keywords: regroup, carry, new ten, new hundred, place value, algorithm
strings.connection: Days 1–4 made new tens and hundreds in our heads. Today we see them in the standard algorithm.
watchFor: Writing 512 for 27 + 35 (not regrouping): ask "Is it about 60 or about 500?" and show the 12 ones becoming 1 ten and 2 ones.
Carrying without knowing why: ask "What does that little 1 stand for: one, ten, or hundred?"
Preferring a mental strategy: great. Ask them to show where their new ten is in the algorithm.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "In the algorithm, what is the carried 1 really worth?" Land: it is a new ten (or hundred) made from 10 ones (or 10 tens), the same thing we did on the number line.

problems.notes: Look for: 7 + 3 + 2, or a known fact. Ask: "How many tens and ones is 12?"
Look for: 27 + 3 + 2. Ask: "Where did the new ten come from?" Model: numberline 27 +3 +2
Look for: 50 + 12, or the algorithm. Ask: "In the algorithm, where is the 12?" Model: column 27 + 35 Model: text 7 + 5 = 12 ones = 1 ten and 2 ones
Look for: the same as 27 + 35, plus 100. Ask: "What is the same in the algorithm?" Model: column 127 + 35
Look for: two regroups (ones and tens). Ask: "How many new tens? How many new hundreds?" Model: column 168 + 57 Model: numberline 168 +32 +25
Look for: the same regroups as 168 + 57, plus 100. Ask: "Predict the answer from the last problem." Model: column 268 + 157
Look for: 400 + 226 - 1 (Day 4!), or the algorithm with three regroups. Ask: "Which way was easier here, and why?" Model: numberline 399 +1 +225, and column 399 + 226

strings.title: Make the Next Whole
strings.label: Day 1
strings.strategy: Add up to the next whole number first, then add what is left.
strings.keywords: next whole, tenths, hundredths, make a one, break apart
strings.connection: Like "make the next ten" with whole numbers, but now 10 tenths or 100 hundredths make a one. Curriculum: B1.5, B2.3, B2.4.
watchFor: Adding digits as if they were whole numbers (2.7 + 0.5 = 2.12): ask "Is 2.12 more or less than 3?" and "How many tenths make a one?"
Lining up the last digits instead of place value (3.75 + 0.4 = 3.79): ask "Is 0.4 four tenths or four hundredths?"
Not knowing decimal partners of 1 (0.7 and 0.3, 0.75 and 0.25): keep the first problems on the board and point back to them.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How is this like making the next ten?" Land: get to the next whole, then add the rest. Ten tenths (or 100 hundredths) make one whole.

problems.notes: Look for: 7 tenths and 3 tenths make 10 tenths. Ask: "How many tenths make one whole?" Model: numberline 0.7 +0.3

responses.say: 7 tenths and 3 tenths is 10 tenths, that's 1.

responses.tip: Ask: why is it 1.0 and not 10?
Ask: is 0.10 more or less than 0.7? How many tenths make a whole?

problems.notes: Look for: "0.7 and 0.3 make a whole." Ask: "How does the first problem help?" Model: numberline 2.7 +0.3

responses.say: 2.7 is 27 tenths, plus 3 tenths is 30 tenths.

responses.tip: Ask: is the answer more or less than 2.7?

problems.notes: Look for: 2.7 + 0.3 = 3, then 0.2 more. Ask: "Where did the 0.5 go?" Word choice: "I broke 0.5 into 0.3 and 0.2." Model: numberline 2.7 +0.3 +0.2

responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: where did the 0.5 go?
Then ask: is there a jump that gets you to a whole?
Added tenths like whole numbers. Ask: is 2.12 more or less than 2.7?

problems.notes: Look for: 75 + 25 = 100 hundredths. Ask: "How is this like 75¢ + 25¢?" Model: numberline 0.75 +0.25

responses.say: 75 hundredths and 25 hundredths is 100 hundredths, that's 1.
Three quarters and a quarter make a dollar.
responses.tip: Money is a great bridge. Name it.
Ask: how many hundredths make a whole?

problems.notes: Look for: 3.75 + 0.25 = 4, then 0.15 more. Ask: "What do you need to get from 3.75 to 4?" Model: numberline 3.75 +0.25 +0.15

responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: how did you split 0.4?
Accept and connect to tenths.
Added 4 hundredths, not 4 tenths. Ask: is 0.4 closer to 0 or to a half?

problems.notes: Look for: 4.86 + 0.14 = 5, then 0.16 more. Ask: "What is the next whole after 4.86?" Model: numberline 4.86 +0.14 +0.16

responses.tip: Adding the tenths only. Good place-value thinking.
Added 3 hundredths. Ask: is 0.3 three tenths or three hundredths?

problems.notes: Look for: 6.95 + 0.05 = 7, then 1.15 more. Ask: "Can the last problems help?" Model: numberline 6.95 +0.05 +1.15

responses.tip: Two good jumps. Ask: where did you cross a whole?
Lined up the last digits. Ask: about how big should the answer be?

strings.title: Add a Friendly Number, Then Adjust
strings.label: Day 2
strings.strategy: When a decimal is close to a whole number, add the whole number, then take back the extra.
strings.keywords: friendly number, close to, take back, adjust, compensate
strings.connection: Day 1 got to the next whole. Today we round a number up to a whole and fix it at the end. Curriculum: B2.3, B2.4.
watchFor: Adjusting the wrong way (3.99 + 2.45 = 6.46): ask "Did you add too much or too little? So do you take back or add on?"
Taking back the wrong amount (taking back 0.1 instead of 0.01): ask "How far is 3.99 from 4?"
Rounding both numbers and forgetting to fix both: ask "How much extra did you add in all?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "When is this strategy a good choice?" Land: when a number is close to a whole, use the whole and adjust. Adding too much means take some back.

problems.notes: Look for: a quick known fact. Ask: "Hold on to this answer." Model: numberline 2.45 +4
Look for: 4 + 2.45 = 6.45, then back 0.01. Ask: "How is 3.99 different from 4?" Word choice: "I added 0.01 too much, so I took it back." Model: numberline 2.45 +4 -0.01

responses.say: 4 + 2.45 is 6.45, but I added 0.01 too much, so 6.44.
responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: why take back and not add on?
Give and take. Name it and compare.
Adjusted the wrong way. Ask: did you add too much or too little?

problems.notes: Look for: a quick fact. Ask: "What's the friendly number here?" Model: numberline 1.36 +6
Look for: 6 + 1.36 = 7.36, then back 0.1. Ask: "How far is 5.9 from 6?" Model: numberline 1.36 +6 -0.1

responses.tip: Took back a hundredth. Ask: is 5.9 one tenth or one hundredth away from 6?

problems.notes: Look for: 3 + 3.47 = 6.47, then back 0.02. Ask: "Which number is close to a whole?" Model: numberline 3.47 +3 -0.02

responses.tip: Works, but ask: which way was quicker?
Adjusted the wrong way. Ask: did 3 add too much or too little?

problems.notes: Look for: 5 + 5 = 10, then back 0.02 (0.01 for each). Ask: "How much extra did you add in all?" Model: numberline 0 +5 +5 -0.02

responses.say: 5 + 5 is 10, I added 0.01 too much twice, so 9.98.

responses.tip: Took back only one extra. Ask: how many numbers did you round?

problems.notes: Look for: 2 + 3.8 = 5.8, then back 0.05. Ask: "How far is 1.95 from 2?" Model: numberline 3.8 +2 -0.05

responses.tip: Day 1's strategy. Ask: which is quicker for you?
Adjusted the wrong way. Ask: did adding 2 add too much or too little?

strings.title: Subtraction as Distance
strings.label: Day 3
strings.strategy: Find the difference by adding up from the smaller number to the larger one, through friendly numbers.
strings.keywords: difference, distance, add up, how far, friendly number
strings.connection: Uses Day 1's make-the-next-whole jumps to find how far apart two numbers are. Curriculum: B2.3, B2.4.
watchFor: Subtracting the smaller digit from the larger in each place (5 − 2.75 = 3.75 or 3.35): ask "Is the gap from 2.75 to 5 more or less than 3?"
Forgetting a jump when adding up: ask "Show me each jump. Add up the jumps."
Answering with the end point instead of the distance: ask "Where did you land, and how far did you go?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "When is adding up easier than taking away?" Land: subtraction can be the distance between two numbers; jump through friendly numbers and add up the jumps.

problems.notes: Look for: "0.25 gets from 2.75 to 3." Ask: "How far apart are they?" Model: numberline 2.75 ~3

responses.say: Like $3 minus $2.75, you get a quarter back.

problems.notes: Look for: 2.75 to 3 is 0.25, then 3 to 5 is 2. Ask: "Can the last problem help?" Word choice: "The distance from 2.75 to 5 is 2.25." Model: numberline 2.75 >3 >5

responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: add up the jumps.

responses.say: 5 − 3 is 2, but I took away 0.25 too much, so 2.25.
responses.tip: Friendly number from Day 2. Name it.
Subtracted digits the wrong way. Ask: is the gap more or less than 3?

problems.notes: Look for: 2.75 to 3 is 0.25, to 5 is 2, to 5.1 is 0.1. Ask: "What changed from the last problem?" Model: numberline 2.75 >3 >5 >5.1

responses.say: Last one was 2.25, and 5.1 is 0.1 more, so 2.35.
responses.tip: Using the last problem. Celebrate it.
Treated 0.1 as 0.01. Ask: how far is it from 5 to 5.1?

problems.notes: Look for: 1.6 to 2 is 0.4, then 2 to 4 is 2. Ask: "What friendly number is close to 1.6?" Model: numberline 1.6 >2 >4

responses.tip: Ask: is 1.6 more or less than 2? So is the answer more or less than 2?

problems.notes: Look for: 3.8 to 4 is 0.2, 4 to 6 is 2, 6 to 6.02 is 0.02. Ask: "Where are your friendly stops?" Model: numberline 3.8 >4 >6 >6.02

responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: add up the jumps.
Subtracted digits the wrong way. Ask: about how big is the gap?

problems.notes: Look for: 7.45 to 7.5 to 8 to 10. Ask: "How can you get to a whole number quickly?" Model: numberline 7.45 >8 >10

responses.tip: Smaller steps work. Ask: can you combine them?
Ask: is 7.45 closer to 7 or 8? So about how big is the gap?

problems.notes: Look for: the numbers are close, so adding up is quick. Ask: "Why is adding up a good choice here?" Model: numberline 6.85 >7 >7.3

responses.tip: Ask: are 7.3 and 6.85 more than one whole apart?

strings.title: Constant Difference
strings.label: Day 4
strings.strategy: Slide both numbers by the same amount so the one you subtract becomes a whole number; the difference stays the same.
strings.keywords: same difference, slide, shift both, friendly number
strings.connection: Day 3 found the distance on a number line. Today we slide that distance to an easier place. Curriculum: B2.1, B2.3, B2.4.
watchFor: Sliding only one number (4.03 − 1.98 → 4.03 − 2): ask "If you move only one number, does the gap stay the same?"
Sliding in opposite directions: ask "Which way did each number move?"
Subtracting the smaller digit from the larger (4.03 − 1.98 = 3.95): ask "About how far is 1.98 from 4?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why does the answer not change when both numbers move?" Land: the gap stays the same, so slide both numbers until the second one is friendly.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "Hold on to this. How far apart are 4 and 2?" Model: numberline 2 ~4
Look for: subtract the 2 ones; the 0.05 stays. Ask: "What changed from the first problem?" Model: numberline 4.05 -2
Look for: slide both up 0.02 to get 4.05 − 2. Ask: "Can the last problem help? How?" Word choice: "I moved both numbers up 0.02, so the gap stayed the same." Model: slide 4.03 - 1.98 > +0.02

responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: why add to both?
Day 3's adding up. Compare the two.
Subtracted the smaller digit from the larger. Ask: about how far is 1.98 from 4?

problems.notes: Look for: slide both up 0.1 to get 6.3 − 3. Ask: "What would make 2.9 friendly?" Model: slide 6.2 - 2.9 > +0.1

responses.tip: Moved only one number. Ask: did the gap stay the same?

problems.notes: Look for: slide both up 0.03 to get 8.17 − 4. Ask: "How much do you slide?" Model: slide 8.14 - 3.97 > +0.03

responses.tip: Day 2's adjust. Ask: why add back?
Adjusted the wrong way. Ask: did taking 4 take away too much or too little?

problems.notes: Look for: slide both up 0.01 to get 5.26 − 2. Ask: "Which number do you want to make friendly?" Model: slide 5.25 - 1.99 > +0.01

responses.tip: Adjusted the wrong way. Ask: did taking 2 take away too much or too little?

problems.notes: Look for: slide both up 0.25 to get 9.75 − 5. Ask: "Is there more than one way to slide?" Model: slide 9.5 - 4.75 > +0.25

responses.tip: Sliding down works too. Ask: which slide is easier?
A great noticing. Ask: how do you know?

strings.title: Estimate, Then Choose
strings.label: Day 5
strings.strategy: Estimate first with friendly numbers, then choose a strategy that fits the numbers and check the answer against the estimate.
strings.keywords: estimate, about, friendly number, reasonable, choose a strategy
strings.connection: Brings together Days 1 to 4. The estimate is a check: is the exact answer reasonable? Curriculum: B2.3 (estimate sums and differences of decimals), B2.4.
watchFor: Skipping the estimate: before anyone solves, ask "About how much? More or less than ...?"
Estimating with the wrong place value (4.5 as 45): ask "Is 4.5 closer to 4 or to 40?"
Using one strategy for everything: ask "Which strategy fits these numbers? Why?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did your estimate help you check your answer?" and "Which strategy did you choose for each, and why?" Land: look at the numbers first, then choose.

problems.notes: First ask: "About how much?" (about 7.5). Look for: 3 + 4.5 = 7.5, back 0.02. Model: estimate 2.98 + 4.5 ≈ 3 + 4.5

responses.tip: Estimate first.
Ask: is 3.43 close to your estimate?

problems.notes: First ask: "About how much?" (about 2). Look for: adding up from 3.97, or sliding to 6.03 − 4. Model: estimate 6 - 3.97 ≈ 6 - 4

responses.tip: Estimate first.
Ask: is 3.97 close to your estimate of 2?

problems.notes: First ask: "About how much?" (about 6.5). Look for: 3.75 + 0.25 = 4, then 2.35 more. Model: estimate 3.75 + 2.6 ≈ 4 + 2.5

responses.tip: Estimate first.
Lined up the last digits. Ask: is 5.81 close to your estimate?

problems.notes: First ask: "About how much?" (about 2). Look for: slide up 0.01 to get 7.03 − 5. Model: estimate 7.02 - 4.99 ≈ 7 - 5

responses.tip: Estimate first.
Moved only one number. Ask: did the gap stay the same?

problems.notes: First ask: "About how much?" (about 3). Look for: adding up 9.75 → 10 → 12.5. Model: estimate 12.5 - 9.75 ≈ 12.5 - 10

responses.tip: Estimate first.
Ask: is 9.75 more or less than 10? So is the gap more or less than 2.5?

problems.notes: First ask: "About how much?" (about 6). Look for: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6, back 0.03. Model: estimate 1.99 + 1.99 + 1.99 ≈ 2 + 2 + 2

responses.tip: Estimate first.

responses.say: 6, but 0.01 too much three times, so 5.97.

responses.tip: Took back only one extra. Ask: how many numbers did you round?

problems.notes: First ask: "About how much?" (about 7.75 or 8). Look for: 8.4 − 0.4 = 8, then − 0.25. Model: estimate 8.4 - 0.65 ≈ 8.5 - 0.5

responses.tip: Estimate first.
Took 4 from 6 in the tenths. Ask: is 8.25 more than 8.4 − 0.5?

strings.title: Split a Factor
strings.label: Day 1
strings.strategy: Split one factor into friendly parts (like 10 and 2), multiply each part, then add the products.
strings.keywords: split, partial products, distributive property, ten and some more
strings.connection: Builds on facts to 10 × 10. Facts to 12 × 12 come from a ten fact plus a small fact. Curriculum: B2.1 (distributive property), B2.2 (facts to 12 × 12).
watchFor: Splitting both factors and multiplying only matching parts (12 × 7 as 10 × 7 + 2 = 72): ask "Did every part of 12 get multiplied by 7?"
Adding instead of multiplying a part (12 × 7 = 70 + 2 + 7): draw the area model and ask "What is the area of the small piece?"
Skip counting from 0 every time: accept it, then ask "Is there a fact you already know that's close?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did 10 × and 2 × help you with 12 ×?" Land: split a factor into friendly parts, multiply each part, and add. The area model shows every piece.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: array 7 x 10
Look for: a double. Ask: "Hold on to this one too." Model: array 7 x 2
Look for: 10 × 7 + 2 × 7 = 70 + 14. Ask: "How did the first two help?" Word choice: "I split 12 into 10 and 2." Model: area 10+2 x 7

responses.say: 10 sevens is 70 and 2 sevens is 14, so 84.
responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: where are the 70 and the 14?

responses.say: I see it in the dots: a 10 part and a 2 part.

responses.tip: Using a known fact. Accept it.
Only multiplied the 10. Ask: did every part of 12 get multiplied by 7?

problems.notes: Look for: 10 × 8 + 2 × 8 = 80 + 16. Ask: "Can you split it the same way?" Model: area 10+2 x 8

responses.tip: Doubling. Name it: × 8 is double, double, double.
Ask: what is 2 × 8? Where is that piece in the area model?

problems.notes: Look for: 10 × 9 + 1 × 9 = 90 + 9. Ask: "What friendly split works here?" Model: area 10+1 x 9

responses.tip: Over and back. We'll do more on Day 3.
Ask: is 11 × 9 the same as 10 × 10? Draw both.

problems.notes: Look for: 10 × 12 + 2 × 12 = 120 + 24. Ask: "Which factor did you split?" Model: area 10+2 x 12

responses.tip: Four parts. Ask: why are there four pieces?
Missed two pieces. Draw the area model and ask: what is in the other two boxes?

problems.notes: Look for: 10 × 15 + 2 × 15 = 150 + 30. Ask: "Does splitting still work with bigger numbers?" Model: area 10+2 x 15

responses.tip: Split the other factor. Both work.
A Day 4 strategy. Accept and name it.

strings.title: Area Model with Two Splits
strings.label: Day 2
strings.strategy: Split both factors by place value, find the four partial products, and add them.
strings.keywords: area model, partial products, tens and ones, place value
strings.connection: Day 1 split one factor. Today both factors are split by place value, so the area model has four parts. Curriculum: B2.1, B2.6 (area model and algorithms).
watchFor: Multiplying only tens by tens and ones by ones (14 × 15 = 100 + 20 = 120): ask "How many boxes are in the area model? Did you fill them all?"
Place-value slips in a partial product (10 × 20 = 20): ask "Is that ten twenties?"
Losing track of the partial products: write each one inside its box, then add.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How does the area model show every partial product?" Land: split both factors by place value; there is a product for every box, and the boxes add to the answer.

problems.notes: Look for: a quick ten fact. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: area 10 x 10+5

responses.tip: Ask: why does × 10 make the digits shift?

problems.notes: Look for: 4 × 10 + 4 × 5, or double 15 twice. Ask: "What do you know about 15s?" Model: area 4 x 10+5
Look for: 150 + 60. Ask: "How do the last two help?" Word choice: "14 fifteens is 10 fifteens and 4 fifteens." Model: area 10+4 x 10+5

responses.tip: Uses the helper problems. Ask: where are they?
The target model. Ask: what's in each box?
Missed two boxes. Ask: how many boxes are in the area model?

problems.notes: Look for: 200 + 10 + 60 + 3. Ask: "What are the four boxes?" Model: area 10+3 x 20+1

responses.tip: Split only one factor. Good choice here.
Ask: how many 13s are you adding? 20 or 21?

problems.notes: Look for: 200 + 40 + 40 + 8. Ask: "Is there a way with fewer boxes?" Model: area 20+4 x 10+2

responses.tip: Connect: the algorithm's rows are partial products too.
Missed a box. Ask: show me all four boxes.

problems.notes: Look for: 600 + 90 + 40 + 6. Ask: "Which box is the biggest? About how big is the answer?" Model: area 30+2 x 20+3

responses.tip: Ask: where is 96 in the area model? (the 3 row: 90 + 6)
Missed two boxes. Ask: did every part of 32 get multiplied by every part of 23?

problems.notes: Look for: 200 + 80 + 50 + 20, or 25 × 4 = 100 thinking. Ask: "Which way is quickest?" Model: area 20+5 x 10+4

responses.tip: Uses 4 quarters make a dollar. Name it.

strings.title: Over and Back
strings.label: Day 3
strings.strategy: When a factor is close to a friendly number, multiply by the friendly number, then take away the extra group.
strings.keywords: friendly number, over, take back, one group too many
strings.connection: Like Week 1 Day 2 (add a friendly number, then adjust), but with groups: going over by 1 means one whole group too many. Curriculum: B2.1, B2.6.
watchFor: Taking back 1 instead of one group (19 × 15 = 300 − 1 = 299): ask "How many 15s did you add too many? How much is that?"
Taking back from the wrong factor (19 × 15 = 300 − 19): draw the area model and ask "What is the size of the strip you're taking away?"
Adding the extra group instead of subtracting: ask "Did you make too many groups or too few?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why do we take away 15 and not 1?" Land: 20 × 15 is one group of 15 too many, so take away a whole group.

problems.notes: Look for: 2 × 15 = 30, so 20 × 15 = 300. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: area 20 x 10+5
Look for: 300 − 15. Ask: "How is 19 × 15 different from 20 × 15?" Word choice: "19 fifteens is one fifteen less than 20 fifteens." Model: area 20-1 x 15

responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: what's in the strip we took away?
Splitting works too. Ask: which is quicker?
Took away 1, not one group. Ask: how many 15s too many?

problems.notes: Look for: 2 × 24 = 48, then × 10. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: ratio 1:24, 2:48, 20:480
Look for: 480 − 24. Ask: "How much do you take away this time?" Model: area 20-1 x 24

responses.tip: Shows the subtraction. Good.
Took away a 19. Ask: what is the size of the strip, 19 or 24?

problems.notes: Look for: 30 × 12 = 360, then − 12. Ask: "What's the friendly number?" Model: area 30-1 x 12

responses.tip: Added instead of taking away. Ask: is 29 more or less than 30?

problems.notes: Look for: 30 × 15 = 450, then + 15. Ask: "Over or under this time?" Model: area 30+1 x 15

responses.tip: Under, then add a group. Ask: why add?
Took away when 31 is more than 30. Ask: too many groups or too few?

problems.notes: Look for: 20 × 25 = 500, then − 2 × 25 = 50. Ask: "How many groups too many?" Model: area 20-2 x 25

responses.tip: Tomorrow's strategy. Name it.
Ask: 2 what? How big is each group?

strings.title: Double and Halve
strings.label: Day 4
strings.strategy: Halve one factor and double the other; the product stays the same, and the new problem can be easier.
strings.keywords: double, halve, same area, rearrange, friendly factor
strings.connection: Days 1 to 3 split a factor. Today we change both factors without changing the product. Curriculum: B2.1 (properties of operations), B2.6.
watchFor: Doubling (or halving) both factors (16 × 15 → 32 × 30): cut the rectangle and ask "Did the area stay the same?"
Halving an odd number and getting stuck: ask "Which factor is easier to halve?"
Not seeing when to use it: ask "Which factor would you like to turn into 10, 50 or 100?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why does the product stay the same?" Land: cut the rectangle in half and put the halves together; the area doesn't change. Halve the even factor, double the other, and look for 10s and 100s.

problems.notes: Look for: 8 × 3 = 24, then × 10. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: area 8 x 30
Look for: halve 16, double 15 → 8 × 30. Ask: "Why is it the same answer as the last one?" Word choice: "I halved 16 and doubled 15." Model: halve 16 x 15 = 8 x 30

responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: why is the area the same?
Doubled both. Ask: is 32 × 30 the same area? Draw both rectangles.

problems.notes: Look for: 7 × 50. Ask: "Which factor would you like to double?" Model: halve 14 x 25 = 7 x 50
Look for: 9 × 10. Ask: "What happens when you double 5?" Model: halve 18 x 5 = 9 x 10
Look for: 6 × 70. Ask: "Halve which one?" Model: halve 12 x 35 = 6 x 70

responses.tip: Halved only one. Ask: what did you do to the other factor?

problems.notes: Look for: 12 × 50, then 6 × 100. Ask: "Can you do it again?" Model: halve 24 x 25 = 12 x 50 = 6 x 100

responses.tip: Twice. Ask: why stop at 6 × 100?

problems.notes: Look for: double 15, halve 18 → 30 × 9. Ask: "Which factor do you halve this time?" Model: halve 15 x 18 = 30 x 9

responses.tip: Over and back. Good.

strings.title: Choosing a Strategy
strings.label: Day 5
strings.strategy: Look at the numbers first, then choose: split a factor, go over and back, or double and halve.
strings.keywords: choose, efficient, friendly numbers, split, over and back, double and halve
strings.connection: Brings together Days 1 to 4. Curriculum: B2.1, B2.2, B2.6.
watchFor: Using the same strategy for every problem: ask "What do you notice about these numbers before you start?"
Forgetting to adjust after going over: ask "How many groups too many?"
Not checking reasonableness: ask "About how big should the answer be?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Which strategy did you choose for each problem, and what about the numbers made you choose it?" Land: numbers near a ten → over and back; an even factor and a 5 or 25 → double and halve; otherwise split by place value.

problems.notes: Look for: double and halve to 100 × 4. Ask: "What do you notice about 25?" Model: halve 25 x 16 = 50 x 8 = 100 x 4

responses.say: 4 quarters in a dollar, 16 is 4 fours: 400.

problems.notes: Look for: 230 + 23. Ask: "What's friendly about 11?" Model: area 10+1 x 23

responses.tip: Ask: how many 23s? Show the extra strip.

problems.notes: Look for: 20 × 12 − 12. Ask: "Which number is close to a friendly number?" Model: area 20-1 x 12

responses.tip: Ask: one what? How big is the group?

problems.notes: Look for: 7 × 70. Ask: "Is there an even factor to halve?" Model: halve 14 x 35 = 7 x 70
Look for: 20 × 13 + 13. Ask: "Have we seen these numbers before?" (13 × 21 on Day 2). Model: area 20+1 x 13

responses.say: It's the same as 13 × 21 from Tuesday.
responses.tip: Commutative property. Name it.

problems.notes: Look for: 50 × 12 − 12. Ask: "What's the friendly number?" Model: area 50-1 x 12

responses.tip: Ask: how many 12s too many?

problems.notes: Look for: 18 × 50, 9 × 100. Ask: "How many times can you halve 36?" Model: halve 36 x 25 = 18 x 50 = 9 x 100

strings.title: 50% and 25%: Halve It
strings.label: Day 1
strings.group: Grade 6 · Week 1 · Percents of Whole Numbers
strings.strategy: 50% is half, and 25% is half of a half, so find them by halving.
strings.keywords: percent, per hundred, half, quarter, halve, benchmark
strings.connection: Connects percents to fractions students already know: 50% = 1/2 and 25% = 1/4. Curriculum: B1.6 (fractions, decimals, percents), B2.3 (mental math: 25%, 50%).
watchFor: Dividing by the percent (25% of 80 = 80 ÷ 25 = 3.2): ask "Should 25% of 80 be more or less than half of 80?"
Subtracting the percent (25% of 80 = 55): ask "Is 25% a part of the 80 or an amount to take away?"
Thinking 75% needs a new start: ask "How many 25%s make 75%?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did 50% help with 25%?" Land: 100% is the whole, 50% is half, 25% is half of that. Halving is a fast way to find these percents.

problems.notes: Look for: half of 80. Ask: "What does 50% mean?" Word choice: "50 out of every 100, so half." Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 50:40, 100:80

responses.say: 50% is half, and half of 80 is 40.
responses.tip: The target model. Ask: where is 100%?
Divided by the percent. Ask: should 50% of 80 be bigger or smaller than 2?

problems.notes: Look for: half of 40. Ask: "How does 50% help?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 25:20, 50:40, 100:80

responses.say: Half of 80 is 40, half of 40 is 20.
responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: why halve twice?

responses.say: Like 4 quarters in a dollar: 80 split into 4.

responses.tip: Divided by the percent. Ask: is 25% of 80 more or less than half of 80?

problems.notes: Look for: half of 36. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 50:18, 100:36

responses.say: Half of 30 is 15, half of 6 is 3: 18.

problems.notes: Look for: half of 18. Ask: "How did the last one help?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 25:9, 50:18, 100:36

responses.tip: Subtracted. Ask: is 25% an amount to take away, or a part of 36?

problems.notes: Look for: half of 140 is 70, half of 70 is 35. Ask: "Halve, then halve again?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 25:35, 50:70, 100:140

responses.tip: Split the whole. Good thinking.
Subtracted. Ask: should 25% of 140 be more or less than half of 140?

problems.notes: Look for: 3 × 9, or 36 − 9. Ask: "How many 25%s make 75%?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 25:9, 50:18, 75:27, 100:36

responses.tip: Take away a quarter. Name it.

problems.notes: Look for: half of 45. Ask: "What is half of 45?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 25:22.5, 50:45, 100:90

responses.tip: Ask: can we share the 2 that's left? What's half of 1?

strings.title: 10% and 1%
strings.label: Day 2
strings.group: Grade 6 · Week 1 · Percents of Whole Numbers
strings.strategy: 10% is one tenth (divide by 10) and 1% is one hundredth (divide by 100).
strings.keywords: percent, tenth, hundredth, divide by 10, divide by 100, place value
strings.connection: Day 1 halved. Today we divide by 10 and 100 and see the digits shift. Curriculum: B1.6, B2.3 (mental math: 1%, 10%).
watchFor: Mixing up 10% and 1% (10% of 350 = 3.5): ask "Is 10% a tenth or a hundredth?"
Dropping a zero that isn't there (10% of 64 = 6): ask "What is 64 ÷ 10? What happens to the 4?"
Thinking 1% is always 1: ask "Is 1% of 400 the same as 1% of 4?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How are 10% and 1% related?" Land: 10% is one tenth (÷ 10), and 1% is a tenth of that (÷ 100). Then build other percents from them.

problems.notes: Look for: 400 ÷ 10. Ask: "What does 10% mean?" Model: ratio percent:amount, 100:400, 10:40
Look for: 40 ÷ 10, or 400 ÷ 100. Ask: "How does 10% help?" Model: ratio percent:amount, 100:400, 10:40, 1:4

responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: why ÷ 10 again?
Ask: is 1% of 400 the same as 1% of 100?

problems.notes: Look for: 350 ÷ 10. Ask: "What happens to the digits?" Model: ratio percent:amount, 100:350, 10:35

responses.tip: Found 1%. Ask: is 10% a tenth or a hundredth?

problems.notes: Look for: 35 ÷ 10. Ask: "Can you divide 35 by 10?" Model: ratio percent:amount, 100:350, 10:35, 1:3.5

responses.say: 10% is 35, a tenth of that is 3.5.

responses.tip: Stopped at 10%. Ask: is 1% more or less than 10%?

problems.notes: Look for: 64 ÷ 10 = 6.4. Ask: "What happens to the 4?" Model: ratio percent:amount, 100:64, 10:6.4

responses.tip: Dropped the 4. Ask: what is 4 ÷ 10?

problems.notes: Look for: 1% is 3.5, double it. Ask: "Which percent from today helps?" Model: ratio percent:amount, 100:350, 1:3.5, 2:7

responses.say: 10% is 35, 2% is a fifth of that: 7.

problems.notes: Look for: 10% + 1% = 40 + 4. Ask: "Can you build 11% from today's percents?" Model: ratio percent:amount, 100:400, 10:40, 1:4, 11:44

responses.tip: Ask: should 11% of 400 be more or less than 400?

strings.title: 5% and 15%
strings.label: Day 3
strings.group: Grade 6 · Week 1 · Percents of Whole Numbers
strings.strategy: 5% is half of 10%, and 15% is 10% + 5%.
strings.keywords: percent, half of 10%, build up, combine, tip
strings.connection: Combines Day 1 (halving) and Day 2 (10%). Useful for tips and taxes. Curriculum: B2.3 (mental math: 5%, 15%).
watchFor: Dividing by 5 for 5% (5% of 60 = 12): ask "Is 5% more or less than 10%?"
Adding the percent to the number (15% of 80 = 95): ask "Is 15% a part of 80 or extra?"
Losing track when building 15%: write each part on the double number line.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did 10% help with 5% and 15%?" Land: find 10%, halve it for 5%, then add them for 15%.

problems.notes: Look for: 60 ÷ 10. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 10:6, 100:60
Look for: half of 10%. Ask: "How does 10% help?" Word choice: "5% is half of 10%." Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 5:3, 10:6, 100:60

responses.say: 10% is 6, so 5% is half of that: 3.
responses.tip: The target strategy.
Divided by 5. Ask: is 5% more or less than 10%?

problems.notes: Look for: 6 + 3. Ask: "Can you build 15% from the last two?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 5:3, 10:6, 15:9, 100:60

responses.tip: Added the percent. Ask: should 15% of 60 be more or less than 60?

problems.notes: Look for: 10% = 8, 5% = 4, 15% = 12. Ask: "Same steps?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 5:4, 10:8, 15:12, 100:80

responses.say: 10% is 8, and 15% is one and a half times that.

responses.tip: Ask: is 15% a part of 80 or extra?

problems.notes: Look for: 10% = 24, half is 12. Ask: "What's 10% first?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 5:12, 10:24, 100:240

responses.tip: Divided by 5. That's 20%. Ask: is 5% more or less than 10%?

problems.notes: Look for: 24 + 12. Ask: "How did the last one help?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 5:12, 10:24, 15:36, 100:240
Look for: 3 + 1.5. Ask: "What would a 15% tip on $30 be?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 5:1.5, 10:3, 15:4.5, 100:30

responses.tip: Ask: should a 15% tip be more or less than the meal?

strings.title: Build from 10% and 25%
strings.label: Day 4
strings.group: Grade 6 · Week 1 · Percents of Whole Numbers
strings.strategy: Use a benchmark percent you know (10% or 25%) and multiply or combine it to get the percent you need.
strings.keywords: benchmark, build up, multiply, 20%, 30%, 75%, 90%
strings.connection: Days 1 to 3 found single benchmarks. Today we scale them: 30% is 3 × 10%, 75% is 3 × 25%. Curriculum: B2.3, B2.12.
watchFor: Dividing by the percent (20% of 70 = 70 ÷ 20 = 3.5): ask "Should 20% be more or less than 10%?"
Not seeing 90% as 100% − 10%: ask "Is 90% close to a percent you know?"
Losing the whole: keep 100% labeled on the double number line.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Which benchmark did you start from for each one?" Land: start from 10% or 25%, then multiply, add, or subtract from 100%.

problems.notes: Look for: 70 ÷ 10. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 10:7, 100:70
Look for: 2 × 7. Ask: "How many 10%s in 20%?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 10:7, 20:14, 100:70

responses.tip: The target strategy.
A fraction connection. Name it.
Divided by the percent. Ask: should 20% be more or less than 10%?

problems.notes: Look for: 3 × 7. Ask: "Can you keep going?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 10:7, 20:14, 30:21, 100:70

responses.tip: Subtracted the percent. Ask: is 30% a part of 70?

problems.notes: Look for: half of half of 120. Ask: "Which benchmark is this?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 25:30, 50:60, 100:120
Look for: 3 × 30, or 120 − 30. Ask: "How did the last problem help?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 25:30, 50:60, 75:90, 100:120

responses.tip: Subtracted the percent. Ask: is 75% more or less than half?

problems.notes: Look for: 10% = 4.5, × 4 = 18; or 20% = 9, × 2. Ask: "Which benchmark is easiest here?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 10:4.5, 20:9, 40:18, 100:45

responses.tip: Building down. Nice.

problems.notes: Look for: 100% − 10% = 70 − 7. Ask: "Is 90% close to a percent you know?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 10:7, 90:63, 100:70

responses.tip: Ask: what does 90% of something mean? Is it most of it?

strings.title: Choosing a Percent Strategy
strings.label: Day 5
strings.group: Grade 6 · Week 1 · Percents of Whole Numbers
strings.strategy: Look at the percent and the number, then choose: halve, divide by 10 or 100, or build from benchmarks.
strings.keywords: benchmark, choose, combine, 1%, 5%, 10%, 25%, 50%
strings.connection: Brings together Days 1 to 4. Curriculum: B2.3, B2.12.
watchFor: Using only one benchmark for everything: ask "Is there a quicker benchmark for this one?"
Not checking reasonableness: ask "Is the answer more or less than half? Should it be?"
Missing that a% of b = b% of a (60% of 25 = 25% of 60): ask "What if we switch the numbers?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Which benchmark did you use for each, and why?" Land: find a benchmark (50%, 25%, 10%, 5%, 1%) and build from it. Check that the answer makes sense.

problems.notes: Look for: 25% + 10% = 20 + 8, or 3 × 10% + 5%. Ask: "Which benchmarks make 35%?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 10:8, 25:20, 35:28, 100:80

responses.tip: Ask: should 35% of 80 be more or less than half of 80?

problems.notes: Look for: 10% + 2 × 1% = 20 + 4. Ask: "Can 1% help?" Model: ratio percent:amount, 100:200, 10:20, 1:2, 12:24
Look for: 50% − 5% = 30 − 3. Ask: "Is 45% close to a benchmark?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 5:3, 45:27, 50:30, 100:60

responses.tip: Building down from 50%.
Ask: should 45% of 60 be close to half of 60?

problems.notes: Look for: 10% = 2.5, × 6; or 25% of 60 = 15. Ask: "What if you switch the numbers?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 10:2.5, 20:5, 60:15, 100:25

responses.say: It's the same as 25% of 60, a quarter of 60: 15.
responses.tip: Great noticing. Ask: why does switching work?

problems.notes: Look for: 25% + 1% = 12.5 + 0.5. Ask: "Which benchmark is close to 26%?" Model: ratio percent:amount, 100:50, 25:12.5, 1:0.5, 26:13

responses.say: 50 is half of 100, so 26% of 50 is half of 26.
responses.tip: Great connection to "per hundred".
Ask: should 26% of 50 be more or less than half of 50?

problems.notes: Look for: 100% − 1% = 300 − 3. Ask: "Is 99% close to a percent you know?" Model: ratio percent:amount, 100:300, 1:3, 99:297
Look for: 3 × 12, or 48 − 12. Ask: "Which benchmark do you start from?" Model: doubleline percent:amount, 0:0, 25:12, 75:36, 100:48

strings.title: Halves, Quarters and Thirds on the Clock
strings.label: Day 1
strings.group: Grade 6 · Week 2 · Adding and Subtracting Fractions
strings.strategy: Think of fractions as parts of an hour: change each fraction to minutes, add the minutes, then change back.
strings.keywords: fraction of an hour, minutes, common unit, unlike denominators
strings.connection: Students know 1/2 hour = 30 min and 1/4 hour = 15 min. Minutes are a common unit, so unlike denominators can be added. Curriculum: B2.5 (unlike denominators).
watchFor: Adding numerators and denominators (1/2 + 1/4 = 2/6): ask "Is 2/6 more or less than 1/2? Can the sum be smaller than one of the parts?"
Mixing up minutes and the fraction (35 minutes = 35/100): ask "How many minutes in a whole hour?"
Answers over 1 written as improper only: accept, then ask "How many whole hours is that?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why did minutes make these easy?" Land: minutes are a common unit (sixtieths). To add unlike fractions, change them to the same unit first.

problems.notes: Look for: 30 + 15 = 45 minutes, 3/4 of an hour. Ask: "How many minutes is each?" Model: clock 1/2 + 1/4

responses.say: 30 minutes and 15 minutes is 45 minutes, that's 3/4.
responses.tip: The target model.
Added tops and bottoms. Ask: is 2/6 more or less than 1/2?

problems.notes: Look for: 15 + 20 = 35 minutes. Ask: "What fraction of an hour is 35 minutes?" Word choice: "35 out of 60 minutes, that's 7/12." Model: clock 1/4 + 1/3

responses.tip: Ask: how do you know 35 minutes is 7/12?
Twelfths: 5-minute chunks. Connect.
Ask: is 2/7 more or less than 1/3?

problems.notes: Look for: 30 + 20 = 50 minutes. Ask: "How far from a whole hour?" Model: clock 1/2 + 1/3

responses.tip: Ask: is 2/5 more or less than 1/2?

problems.notes: Look for: 40 + 15 = 55 minutes. Ask: "Is it more or less than an hour?" Model: clock 2/3 + 1/4

responses.tip: Ask: is 3/7 more or less than 2/3?

problems.notes: Look for: 45 + 30 = 75 minutes, 1 hour and 15 minutes. Ask: "What happens when we pass the hour?" Model: clock 3/4 + 1/2

responses.tip: Make the next whole, like with decimals.
Ask: 3/4 is already most of an hour. Can adding 1/2 give less than 1?

problems.notes: Look for: 40 + 30 = 70 minutes. Ask: "How much past the hour?" Model: clock 2/3 + 1/2

responses.tip: Correct! Ask: how many whole hours in 7/6?

problems.notes: Look for: 45 + 40 = 85 minutes. Ask: "How many minutes past the hour?" Model: clock 3/4 + 2/3

strings.title: Sixths and Twelfths
strings.label: Day 2
strings.group: Grade 6 · Week 2 · Adding and Subtracting Fractions
strings.strategy: Sixths are 10 minutes and twelfths are 5 minutes; use minutes (or twelfths) as the common unit.
strings.keywords: sixths, twelfths, fifths, minutes, common denominator, equivalent fractions
strings.connection: Day 1 used halves, quarters and thirds. Today: smaller parts. Notice that twelfths are 5-minute chunks, so they work like a common denominator. Curriculum: B2.5.
watchFor: Adding numerators and denominators (1/6 + 1/3 = 2/9): ask "Is 2/9 more or less than 1/3?"
Not simplifying (30/60, 6/12) and thinking it's a different number: ask "Is 30 minutes the same as half an hour?"
Wrong minutes for a sixth (1/6 = 6 minutes): ask "How many sixths in an hour? So how many minutes each?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How are minutes like a common denominator?" Land: change each fraction to the same unit (minutes, sixtieths, or twelfths), add, then simplify.

problems.notes: Look for: 10 + 20 = 30 minutes. Ask: "How many minutes is a sixth?" Model: clock 1/6 + 1/3

responses.tip: Ask: is 2/9 more or less than 1/3?

problems.notes: Look for: 10 + 15 = 25 minutes. Ask: "What fraction is 25 minutes?" Model: clock 1/6 + 1/4

responses.tip: Ask: is 2/10 more or less than 1/4?

problems.notes: Look for: 50 + 5 = 55 minutes. Ask: "How many minutes is a twelfth?" Model: clock 5/6 + 1/12

responses.tip: Ask: is 6/18 more or less than 5/6?

problems.notes: Look for: 25 + 20 = 45 minutes. Ask: "Where have we seen 45 minutes?" Model: clock 5/12 + 1/3

responses.tip: Correct! Ask: is there a simpler name for 9/12?

problems.notes: Look for: 50 + 15 = 65 minutes. Ask: "How far past the hour?" Model: clock 5/6 + 1/4

responses.tip: Ask: 5/6 is almost an hour. Can adding 1/4 give less than 1?

problems.notes: Look for: 35 + 50 = 85 minutes. Ask: "How many minutes past the hour?" Model: clock 7/12 + 5/6
Look for: 12 + 10 = 22 minutes. Ask: "What fraction of 60 is 22?" Model: clock 1/5 + 1/6

responses.tip: Thirtieths are 2-minute chunks.
Ask: is 2/11 more or less than 1/5?

strings.title: Subtracting on the Clock
strings.label: Day 3
strings.group: Grade 6 · Week 2 · Adding and Subtracting Fractions
strings.strategy: Change both fractions to minutes, find the difference, then change back to a fraction of an hour.
strings.keywords: difference, take away, how much more, minutes, common unit
strings.connection: Days 1 and 2 added. The same common unit works for subtraction. Curriculum: B2.5.
watchFor: Subtracting numerators and denominators (3/4 − 1/3 = 2/1): ask "Can the answer be bigger than 3/4?"
Subtracting in the wrong order with minutes (20 − 45): ask "Which is more time, 3/4 or 1/3 of an hour?"
Not seeing the same difference (3/4 − 1/3 and 2/3 − 1/4 are both 25 minutes): ask "Why are these the same?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How is subtracting fractions like adding them?" Land: same unit first (minutes or twelfths), then subtract. The clock shows how much time is left.

problems.notes: Look for: 60 − 15 = 45 minutes. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: clock 1 - 1/4

responses.say: An hour minus 15 minutes is 45 minutes: 3/4.

problems.notes: Look for: 45 − 30 = 15 minutes. Ask: "How much more is 3/4 than 1/2?" Model: clock 3/4 - 1/2

responses.tip: Subtraction as distance.
Subtracted tops and bottoms. Ask: can 3/4 − 1/2 be a whole?

problems.notes: Look for: 45 − 20 = 25 minutes. Ask: "How many minutes is each?" Model: clock 3/4 - 1/3

responses.tip: Ask: can the answer be bigger than 3/4?

problems.notes: Look for: 40 − 15 = 25 minutes. Ask: "Why is it the same as the last one?" Model: clock 2/3 - 1/4

responses.tip: Ask: why the same answer? (both fractions moved 5 minutes)
Ask: can the answer be more than 2/3?

problems.notes: Look for: 50 − 15 = 35 minutes. Ask: "Which fraction is more time?" Model: clock 5/6 - 1/4

responses.tip: Ask: is 4/2 more or less than 5/6?

problems.notes: Look for: 60 − 25 = 35 minutes. Ask: "How much is left in the hour?" Model: clock 1 - 5/12
Look for: 30 − 12 = 18 minutes. Ask: "What fraction of an hour is 18 minutes?" Model: clock 1/2 - 1/5

responses.tip: Tenths are 6-minute chunks.
Ask: is half an hour the same as a fifth of an hour?

strings.title: Mixed Numbers
strings.label: Day 4
strings.group: Grade 6 · Week 2 · Adding and Subtracting Fractions
strings.strategy: Work with whole hours and minutes: add or subtract the wholes and the parts, and regroup an hour as 60 minutes when needed.
strings.keywords: mixed number, whole and part, regroup, hours and minutes, make a whole
strings.connection: Days 1 to 3 stayed within an hour or just past. Today we use several hours and regroup. Like decimals in Grade 5: make the next whole. Curriculum: B2.5.
watchFor: Subtracting the smaller fraction from the larger (1 1/2 − 3/4 = 1 1/4): ask "Can you take 3/4 from 1/2? What could you do?"
Forgetting to regroup past the hour (1 1/2 + 3/4 = 1 5/4): accept, then ask "How many whole hours is 5/4?"
Losing the whole numbers: ask "Where are the whole hours?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "When did you need to regroup an hour?" Land: add or subtract wholes and parts; jump to the next whole (or back to the last one) to regroup.

problems.notes: Look for: two halves make a whole. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: numberline 1 1/2 +1/2
Look for: 1 1/2 + 1/2 = 2, then 1/4 more. Ask: "How did the last one help?" Model: numberline 1 1/2 +1/2 +1/4

responses.tip: Make the next whole. The target strategy.
Correct but not regrouped. Ask: how many wholes in 5/4?
Added tops and bottoms. Ask: is the answer more or less than 2?

problems.notes: Look for: 2 + 1 = 3, and 1/3 + 1/2 = 5/6 (20 + 30 minutes). Ask: "Wholes first, then parts?" Model: numberline 2 1/3 +1 +1/2

responses.tip: Ask: is 2/5 more or less than 1/2? So is 3 2/5 too small?

problems.notes: Look for: 1 1/2 − 1/2 = 1, then − 1/4. Ask: "Can you take 3/4 from 1/2?" Model: numberline 1 1/2 -1/2 -1/4

responses.tip: Back to the last whole. The target strategy.
Adding up. Nice.
Subtracted the smaller fraction from the larger. Ask: can you take 3/4 from 1/2?

problems.notes: Look for: 2 1/4 − 1/4 = 2, then − 1/12 (5 minutes). Ask: "How many minutes is each?" Model: clock 2 1/4 - 1/3

responses.tip: Ask: is 1/3 more or less than 1/4? So should the answer be less than 2?

problems.notes: Look for: from 1 2/3 to 2 is 1/3, then 1 more. Ask: "How far is it from 1 2/3 to 3?" Model: numberline 1 2/3 >2 >3

responses.tip: Ask: is 1 2/3 closer to 1 or 2? So is the gap more or less than 2?

problems.notes: Look for: 130 − 45 = 85 minutes. Ask: "Do you need to regroup?" Model: clock 2 1/6 - 3/4

strings.title: Estimate with Benchmarks
strings.label: Day 5
strings.group: Grade 6 · Week 2 · Adding and Subtracting Fractions
strings.strategy: Compare each fraction to 0, 1/2 or 1 to estimate first, then find the exact answer and check it against the estimate.
strings.keywords: benchmark, about, more than half, close to 1, estimate, reasonable
strings.connection: Uses benchmarks to check answers, including eighths and fifths, which don't fit the clock as neatly. Curriculum: B1.3 (compare fractions), B2.5.
watchFor: Adding numerators and denominators (1/2 + 3/8 = 4/10): ask "Is 4/10 more or less than 1/2? Does that make sense?"
Not estimating first: ask "Is it more or less than 1? How do you know?"
Thinking a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction: ask "Which is bigger, 1/8 or 1/2?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did 1/2 and 1 help you check?" Land: estimate with benchmarks first. If the exact answer is far from the estimate, look again.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: numberline 0 +1/2 +1/2
First ask: "More or less than 1?" (less: 3/8 is less than 1/2). Look for: 4/8 + 3/8 = 7/8. Model: numberline 0 +1/2 +3/8

responses.say: Less than 1, because 3/8 is less than 1/2. 4/8 + 3/8 = 7/8.

responses.tip: Using the first problem. Great.
Ask: is 4/10 more or less than 1/2? Can the sum be less than one of the parts?

problems.notes: First ask: "More or less than 1?" (more: 5/8 is more than 1/2). Look for: 1/8 more than 1. Model: numberline 1/2 +1/2 +1/8

responses.tip: Make the next whole.
Ask: is 6/10 more or less than 5/8?

problems.notes: First ask: "More or less than 1?" (more: 3/5 is more than 1/2). Look for: 6/10 + 5/10 = 11/10. Model: numberline 1/2 +1/2 +1/10

responses.tip: Fifths fit the clock (12 minutes).
Ask: is 4/7 more or less than 3/5?

problems.notes: First ask: "About how much?" (about 1 + 3/4). Look for: 7/8 + 1/8 = 1, then 5/8 more. Model: numberline 7/8 +1/8 +5/8

responses.tip: Make the next whole.
Ask: both are close to 1. Can the sum be less than 1?

problems.notes: First ask: "About how much?" (a bit more than 1/4). Look for: 8/10 − 5/10 = 3/10. Model: numberline 1/2 ~4/5

responses.tip: Subtraction as distance.
Ask: can 4/5 − 1/2 be a whole?

problems.notes: First ask: "About how much?" (almost 2). Look for: 1 + 1 = 2, then back 1/12 and 1/8. Model: numberline 0 +1 +1 -1/12 -1/8

responses.tip: Estimate, then adjust.
Ask: both are almost 1. Can the sum be less than 1?

strings.title: Adding Near a Ten
strings.label: Day 1
strings.strategy: Add a friendly number, then take back the extra.
strings.keywords: jump, friendly number, back 1, take back.
strings.connection: First string of the routine. Sets up the open number line and jumps.
watchFor: Forgot to take back (48 on problem 3, 58 on problem 4): ask "Is 38 + 9 more or less than 38 + 10?"
Went the wrong way (49 on problem 3): ask the same question and use the line.
Counting up by ones from 38: accept the answer, then ask "Is there a faster jump?"

problems.notes: Look for: one jump of 10. Ask: "Where did you start and where did you land?"
Look for: one jump of 20, or two jumps of 10. Ask: "How is this like the last one?"
Look for: 38 + 10, then back 1. Ask: "Can 38 + 10 help you with 38 + 9?" Word choice: "jump to 48, then back 1".
Look for: 38 + 20, then back 1. Ask: "What is the same about 38 + 9 and 38 + 19?"
Look for: 38 + 30, then back 1. Ask: "Predict what someone will do."
Look for: 38 + 50, then back 1. Ask: "Before I show it, how might someone solve this?"
Look for: 38 + 100, then back 2. Ask: "How is this like problems 3 to 6? What changed?" Word choice: go over the ten (or hundred), then take back the extra.

strings.title: Give and Take
strings.label: Day 2
strings.strategy: Move an amount from one number to the other so the total stays the same and one number becomes friendly.
strings.keywords: give, take, move, same total, balance.
strings.connection: Day 1 changed one number and fixed the answer afterwards. Day 2 changes both numbers so the answer never changes.
watchFor: Both numbers moved the same way (50 + 27 for 49 + 26): ask "Did the total stay the same?"
Right amount, only one number changed (50 + 26 = 76): ask "Where did the 1 come from?"
"Add one, take one" with no reason: ask "Why does the total stay the same?" Show two jumps, one growing by 1 and one shrinking by 1.
Students who prefer Day 1's method: accept it, then ask for a second way.

problems.notes: Look for: a quick answer. Ask: "Hold on to this answer."
Look for: "same answer as problem 1", or moving 1 from 26 to 49. Ask: "What do you notice about the answer? Why?" Word choice: "give 1 to 49, take 1 from 26".
Look for: moving 2. Ask: "How many does 48 need? Where do they come from?"
Look for: 40 + 35. Ask: "Which number did you make friendly, and why?"
Look for: 60 + 35. Ask: "What changed from problem 4? What happened to the total?"
Look for: 70 + 35. Ask: "How much did you move this time?"
Look for: 200 + 45, or Day 1's way (198 + 50, then back 3). Ask: "Both work. Which is easier here, and why?"

strings.title: Subtraction as Distance
strings.label: Day 3
strings.strategy: Subtraction finds the distance between two numbers. Start at the smaller number and add up to the larger.
strings.keywords: distance, difference, gap, how far, add up.
strings.connection: The jumps from Days 1 and 2 now go from the smaller number up to the larger.
watchFor: Borrowing in their heads (21 or 12 for 100 − 89): ask "Where are 89 and 100 on the line?"
10 on problem 3: the 1 from 89 to 90 was left out. Ask "Did you start at 89 or at 90?"
24 on problem 7 (copying the pattern): ask "Are 1002 and 1000 the same number?"
Taking away instead of adding up: accept it, then ask "Which way was the shorter jump?"

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "How far is 90 from 100?"
Look for: "98 to 100 is 2" instead of taking away 98. Ask: "Is it easier to take away 98 or to see how far 98 is from 100?"
Look for: 89 to 90 (1), then 90 to 100 (10). Ask: "Where did you stop on the way?"
Look for: 76 to 80 (4), then 80 to 100 (20), or one jump from 76 to 100. Ask: "Which stops did you choose, and why?"
Look for: the same gap as problem 4. Ask: "What do you notice about the answer? Why is it the same?" Word choice: "same gap", "same distance".
Look for: the same gap again. Ask: "Predict 5000 − 4976 before I show it."
Look for: the gap from problem 6, plus 2. Ask: "What changed from problem 6? What happened to the answer?" Word choice: "the top number moved up 2, so the gap grew by 2".

strings.title: Constant Difference
strings.label: Day 4
strings.strategy: Sliding both numbers the same amount in the same direction keeps the difference the same. Slide both to make the subtraction friendlier.
strings.keywords: slide, shift, same difference, constant difference.
strings.connection: Day 2 kept the total by moving the numbers in opposite directions. Day 4 keeps the difference by moving both the same way. Day 3, problems 5 and 6 are the first hint.
watchFor: Slid only one number (62 − 50 = 12 for 62 − 49): ask "Did the gap stay the same?" Show both ends moving on the line.
Slid in opposite directions (63 − 48): that is Day 2's move. Ask "Did the difference stay the same?"
"Add 1 to both" with no reason: ask "What happens to the distance between two points if both slide the same way?"
Slid one number, then fixed the answer (62 − 50 = 12, then add 1): this works. Name it as another way.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact.
Look for: the gap is still 4. Ask: "Is this harder than 12 − 8? Why not?"
Look for: 49 to 50 (1), then 50 to 62 (12), or sliding both up 1 to 63 − 50. Ask: "What did you do to make 49 friendlier?"
Look for: the same answer as problem 3. Ask: "What changed from problem 3? What happened to the answer? Why?" Word choice: "I slid both numbers up 1, so the difference stayed the same".
Look for: sliding both up 1 to 163 − 150. Ask: "Predict before I show it."
Look for: the same slide. Ask: "Does the answer depend on how big the numbers are, or how far apart they are?"
Look for: sliding both up 2 to 73 − 40, or adding up 38 to 40 to 71 (2 + 31). Ask: "Can you slide and add up? Which was quicker?"

strings.title: Choosing a Strategy
strings.label: Day 5
strings.strategy: Choose between adding up (distance) and sliding both numbers (same difference), based on the numbers.
strings.keywords: add up, slide, friendly number, efficient, choose.
strings.connection: Combines Days 3 and 4. The question is no longer how, but which.
watchFor: The same strategy for every problem: ask "Could you do it another way? Would it be quicker?"
Mixing up the slide with Day 2's opposite move: ask "Did the difference stay the same?"
Cannot say why they chose: ask "What did you notice about the numbers first?"

problems.notes: Look for: adding up. Ask: "Which strategy did you choose?"
Look for: adding up from 48, or sliding to 54 − 50.
Look for: 38 to 40 to 70 (2 + 30), or sliding to 72 − 40. Ask: "Which did you choose?"
Look for: sliding to 85 − 40, or adding up 39 to 40 to 84 (1 + 44).
Look for: sliding both up 3 to 606 − 300. Ask: "What made this one easy to slide?"
Look for: adding up 385 to 400 to 1000 (15 + 600), or sliding up 15 to 1015 − 400. Ask: "Why might adding up feel easier here?"
Look for: sliding both up 2 to 2402 − 2000. Ask: "Which strategy fits this one? How can you tell from the numbers?"

strings.wrapUp: Ask "What do you look at in the numbers to choose?" Land: if one number is close to a friendly number, add up or slide, and pick whichever you can do fastest.

strings.title: Times 5 as Half of Times 10
strings.label: Day 1
strings.strategy: Multiply by 10 first (easy), then halve to multiply by 5.
strings.keywords: times ten, half, five is half of ten
strings.connection: Week 1 used a friendly number and fixed the answer afterwards. Here the friendly multiplier is 10, and halving fixes it.
watchFor: Halving the wrong number first (18 x 5 as 9 x 5 = 45): ask "Is 18 x 5 about half of 18 x 10, or half of 18?"
Counting by fives or picturing the column method: ask "What would you do for 64 x 5?"
Stuck halving 170 or 340: ask "What is half of 100? Half of 70?" Then add the halves.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why does halving 18 x 10 give 18 x 5?" Land: 5 is half of 10, so 5 groups is half of 10 groups.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "Hold on to this answer."
Look for: half of 80. Ask: "Can 8 x 10 help you with 8 x 5?" Word choice: "half of ten groups is five groups". Model: ratio 1:8, 10:80, 5:40
Look for: a quick answer. Ask: "Hold on to this one too."
Look for: half of 180. Ask: "What is the same as 8 x 5?" Model: ratio 1:18, 10:180, 5:90
Look for: half of 240. Ask: "Predict how someone will do this." Model: ratio 1:24, 10:240, 5:120
Look for: half of 360. Ask: "Where does the 180 come from?" Model: ratio 1:36, 10:360, 5:180
Look for: half of 170. Ask: "What did you do with the 170?" Word choice: "half of 170 is 85". Model: ratio 1:17, 10:170, 5:85
Look for: half of 640. Ask: "Would this work with bigger numbers?" Model: ratio 1:64, 10:640, 5:320

strings.title: Double and Halve
strings.label: Day 2
strings.strategy: Halve one factor and double the other: the product stays the same and one factor becomes friendly.
strings.keywords: double, halve, same product, friendly number
strings.connection: Day 1 used x10 and halved the answer. Day 2 halves one factor and doubles the other, so the answer never changes (like Week 1, Day 2, Give and Take).
watchFor: Halved both numbers (16 x 25 as 8 x 12.5): ask "Did the product stay the same? What did you do to the 25?"
Doubled both numbers: ask "Is 32 x 50 the same size as 16 x 25?"
A move with no reason ("I just halved it"): ask "Why does the answer stay the same?" Show 4 x 25 as 4 groups of 25, regrouped as 2 groups of 50.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "What did you look for in the numbers?" Land: look for a factor you can halve that turns the other factor into a friendly number (25 to 50 to 100).

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact (four quarters). Ask: "Hold on to this answer."
Look for: double 100, or 4 x 50. Ask: "What do you notice about 8 x 25 and 4 x 50?" Model: halve 8 x 25 = 4 x 50 = 2 x 100
Look for: 8 x 50, then 4 x 100. Ask: "How many times did you halve? Why stop there?" Model: halve 16 x 25 = 8 x 50 = 4 x 100
Look for: 6 x 50 = 3 x 100, or 3 x 4 x 25. Ask: "What did you do first?" Model: halve 12 x 25 = 6 x 50 = 3 x 100
Look for: 7 x 50, or 10 x 25 + 4 x 25. Ask: "Both work. Which was quicker, and why?" Model: halve 14 x 25 = 7 x 50
Look for: 9 x 100. Ask: "Which number did you halve? What did the 50 become?" Model: halve 18 x 50 = 9 x 100
Look for: 30 x 6 = 180, or 15 x 10 + 15 x 2. Ask: "Which number would you double here, and why?" Model: halve 15 x 12 = 30 x 6

strings.title: Over and Back
strings.label: Day 3
strings.strategy: Multiply by a friendly number just over, then take back the extra groups.
strings.keywords: over, take back, groups, one less group
strings.connection: Week 1, Day 1 went over a ten and took back the extra. Here we go over to a friendly multiplier and take back whole groups.
watchFor: Took back 1, not 1 group (9 x 7 as 70 - 1 = 69): ask "How many sevens are we taking back?"
Used the wrong direction (9 x 7 as 70 + 7): ask "Is 9 x 7 more or less than 10 x 7?"
Counting by nines: accept the answer, then ask "What would you do for 99 x 5?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "What do you take back each time?" Land: one less than a friendly number means one less group, so take back one copy of the other number.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "Hold on to this."
Look for: 70 - 7. Ask: "Can 10 x 7 help you with 9 x 7?" Word choice: "one less group". Model: array 10-1 x 7
Look for: 80 - 8. Ask: "What is the same as 9 x 7?" Model: array 10-1 x 8
Look for: 70 + 7. Ask: "Over or under 10 groups? What do you add?" Model: array 10+1 x 7
Look for: 20 x 8 = 160, then - 8. Ask: "What are you taking back?" Model: area 20-1 x 8
Look for: 30 x 6 = 180, then - 6. Ask: "Predict what someone will do." Model: area 30-1 x 6
Look for: 50 x 4 = 200, then - 4. Ask: "What is the same about the last three?" Model: area 50-1 x 4
Look for: 100 x 5 = 500, then - 5. Ask: "Would this work with bigger numbers?" Model: area 100-1 x 5

strings.title: Dividing by 5
strings.label: Day 4
strings.strategy: Double the dividend, then divide by 10: dividing by 5 gives the same answer as dividing double by double.
strings.keywords: double, divide by ten, same answer, how many fives
strings.connection: Day 1 halved to multiply by 5. Day 4 does the opposite: double, then divide by 10. Both use 10 as the friendly number.
watchFor: Halved instead of doubled (80 / 5 as 40 / 10 = 4): ask "Is 80 / 5 less than 80 / 10?"
Divided by 10 and stopped (80 / 5 = 8): ask "How many fives fit in 80? Is it as many as tens?"
Divided by 10 first, then doubled (135 / 10 = 13.5, then 27): accept it, name it as another way, and check the 13.5 jump.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why does doubling both numbers keep the answer the same?" Land: 80 / 5 and 160 / 10 ask the same question, how many fives fit, so the answer stays the same.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "Hold on to this."
Look for: double 8, or 160 / 10. Ask: "Why is it more than 80 / 10?" Word choice: "twice as many fives as tens". Model: ratio 80:5, 160:10, 16:1
Look for: 70 / 10. Ask: "What did you do to 35?" Model: ratio 35:5, 70:10, 7:1
Look for: 150 / 10. Ask: "Predict how someone will do this." Model: ratio 75:5, 150:10, 15:1
Look for: 270 / 10. Ask: "How did you double 135?" Word choice: "double the hundred, double the thirty-five". Model: ratio 135:5, 270:10, 27:1
Look for: 480 / 10. Ask: "Is this the same move as Day 1 turned around?" Model: ratio 240:5, 480:10, 48:1
Look for: 840 / 10. Ask: "Would this work with bigger numbers?" Model: ratio 420:5, 840:10, 84:1

strings.title: Choosing a Strategy
strings.label: Day 5
strings.strategy: Choose between half of x10, double and halve, over and back, and double then divide by 10, based on the numbers.
strings.keywords: choose, friendly number, halve, double, over and back
strings.connection: Combines Days 1 to 4. The question is no longer how, but which.
watchFor: The same strategy for every problem: ask "Could you do it another way? Would it be quicker?"
Mixing up directions (halving to divide by 5, doubling to multiply by 5): ask "Does the answer get bigger or smaller?"
Cannot say why they chose: ask "What did you notice about the numbers first?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "What do you look at in the numbers to choose?" Land: look for 5, 25, 50 (halve or double), a number just under a friendly number (over and back), or a division by 5 (double).

problems.notes: Look for: half of 260. Ask: "Which strategy did you choose?" Model: text 26 x 10 = 260 ; half is 130
Look for: 12 x 100, or 24 x 50 = 12 x 100. Ask: "What made 25 easy to work with?" Model: text 48 x 25 = 24 x 50 ; = 12 x 100
Look for: 140 - 14. Ask: "What are you taking back?" Model: text 10 x 14 = 140 ; 140 - 14 = 126
Look for: 390 / 10. Ask: "Which Day 4 move did you use?" Model: text 195 / 5 = 390 / 10 ; = 39
Look for: 240 - 8. Ask: "What made this one easy to adjust?" Model: text 30 x 8 = 240 ; 240 - 8 = 232
Look for: 500 - 10, or half of 980. Ask: "Two good ways. Which feels quicker, and why?" Model: text 100 x 5 = 500 ; 500 - 10 = 490
Look for: 8 x 70, or 4 x 140, or 16 x 30 + 16 x 5. Ask: "Which number did you halve?" Model: halve 16 x 35 = 8 x 70 = 4 x 140
